title: The Mission Is Not Yet Completed: Buying the Khedive's Shares Before Reading the Report on His Books
participants: The First Lord of the Treasury (Mr Disraeli)

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: The skim is the question nobody would answer. Mr Wilson asked "whether the Khedive of Egypt paid a commission to agents in Egypt on the sale of the Canal shares to the English Government; and, if so, the amount of the commission?" The Chancellor "had no information on that subject; but he would be exceedingly surprised if anything of the kind stated in the Question had occurred." The record establishes that the question was put and not answered, and nothing more.
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: The compromise is the order of events, and it is admitted on the floor. The shares had been bought; the vote of £4,080,000 was listed for the following Monday; and on the Friday the Chancellor told the House that "the mission of Mr. Cave is not yet completed". What he offered to lay were the instructions and the covering correspondence — the terms of reference, not the findings. Parliament was asked to pay for an asset before it could read its own government's examination of the seller's solvency.
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: This is the stage with the longest paper trail, and the fog was maintained by two different reasons given five days apart. On 23 March Mr Disraeli said he had now read the Report and would not publish it because "the Khedive has expressed a strong objection to this Report being made public in the present unsettled condition of Egyptian finance; and, considering that much of the information contained in the Report has been supplied by the Khedive himself, and is of a confidential character, we feel bound to respect his wishes in this matter." On 28 March he said "The text of Mr. Cave's Report, I believe, is not yet in the possession of the Khedive of Egypt" and that "no request of that kind has been made by His Highness to the Government" — and the Chancellor, in the same sitting, said the Report "was not founded solely upon information given by the Khedive, but upon that information and other information obtained by my right hon. Friend", and that "It was no part of the duty of my right hon. Friend ... to prepare a Report for the purpose of being published."
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: The windfall is identified by the Government's own envoy, in the House, and it goes to the bondholders. Cave told the Commons on 12 May that he had estimated the cost of converting the debt under his own plan at £2,000,000, "but I calculate that the cost of conversion under the new scheme will be £7,000,000, by far the larger portion of which is given in the form of a bonus to the holders of Treasury bonds—for the purpose, I suppose, of floating the Debt." A five-million-pound increase in the cost of restructuring, most of it handed to existing creditors as the price of placing the new paper.
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: The containment is the gap that stayed open. Working through the £16,000,000 discrepancy between his own figure of £75,000,000 and the Khedive's Decree of 2 May, Cave accounted for most of it and then stopped: "we shall still have between £2,000,000 and £3,000,000 unaccounted for; and I cannot tell without further information whether this is due to any error in the information given to me or whether it is due to increased expenditure since that information was given." No further inquiry appears in what was read. The official who examined the books told the House he could not say whether he had been misled, and the matter rested there.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: The Suez Canal concessions and the firmans granting them, which the Government undertook to lay before the House but which "will take some time", directing Members meanwhile to "Volumes 55 and 56 of Hertslet's State Papers, which are in the Library" — the terms of the asset being bought were available only as a diplomatic compilation.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: A conversion scheme costing £7,000,000 instead of £2,000,000, most of the difference paid as a bonus to Treasury bondholders, and a British equity stake in the canal acquired before the solvency examination was complete. What followed from that stake is outside what was read and is not asserted.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: The debtor's insolvency is what makes his asset cheap; the purchase relieves his immediate shortfall; the relief postpones the reckoning; postponement requires a conversion; the conversion is floated by paying a bonus to the existing creditors, which enlarges the debt that made the asset cheap.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: That the Suez Canal shares were bought in a secret coup financed overnight by the Rothschilds, on inside knowledge that Egypt was about to go bankrupt, with commissions quietly paid to the arrangers.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: Nothing in the record read here names any bank, any financier or any agent, and the one time the commission question was put in the House it was answered with "he had no information on that subject". No house of issue appears in any of these five debates. So the colourful half of the story is simply not evidenced by what was read, and this dossier asserts none of it. What the record does establish is less lurid and harder to explain away, because it is the Government's own account of its own timing, given under questioning across three months: the shares had been bought and the money was to be voted on the Monday while "the mission of Mr. Cave is not yet completed"; the Report, once received, was withheld on the stated ground that the Khedive objected "in the present unsettled condition of Egyptian finance"; five days later the Prime Minister said the Khedive did not yet have the text and had made no such request, while the Chancellor said the Report had never been meant for publication at all; and when the envoy finally answered for his figures he told the House that £2,000,000 to £3,000,000 of the Khedive's debt was "unaccounted for" and that £5,000,000 of the gap was a bonus to Treasury bondholders "for the purpose, I suppose, of floating the Debt." That is a documented asymmetry: the purchaser's own assessment of the seller's books existed, was read by the Cabinet, and was kept from the legislature that paid — for reasons that changed within a week.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: Five exchanges in the House of Commons, February to May 1876, printed in Hansard at vol 227 cc226-7, vol 227 c1120, vol 227 c1870, vol 228 c480, vol 228 cc699-700 and vol 229 cc490-1. They record: that on 11 February the Chancellor of the Exchequer stated Mr Cave's mission to Egypt was "not yet completed" while agreeing to lay only the instructions and antecedent correspondence, with the vote on the Suez Canal shares listed for the following Monday; that on 29 February the question whether the Khedive paid a commission to agents on the sale was answered with no information and an expression of surprise; that on 13 March the First Lord of the Treasury had not yet seen the Report, said to have reached the Foreign Office that afternoon, and invited the Member to repeat the question later; that on 23 March he had read it and refused publication because the Khedive strongly objected in the present unsettled condition of Egyptian finance and because much of the information was his and confidential; that on 28 March he said the Khedive did not yet have the text and had requested nothing, while the Chancellor said the Report was not founded solely on the Khedive's information and had never been intended for publication; and that on 12 May Mr Stephen Cave answered for a £16,000,000 discrepancy between his £75,000,000 estimate and the Khedive's Decree of 2 May, reducing it by £5,000,000 of nearly-repaid loans and £5,000,000 of excess conversion cost — the conversion costing £7,000,000 against his own plan's £2,000,000, "by far the larger portion of which is given in the form of a bonus to the holders of Treasury bonds" — and conceding £2,000,000 to £3,000,000 still unaccounted for, which he could not attribute between error in the information given him and later expenditure. The Report itself was not read.

citations.title: House of Commons, "EGYPT—MISSION OF MR. CAVE—THE PURCHASE OF THE SUEZ CANAL SHARES.—QUESTIONS.", HC Deb 11 February 1876 vol 227 cc226-7 (Historic Hansard)
citations.quoteOrFact: Read in full on Parliament's own Historic Hansard service. THE SEQUENCE THIS CITATION FIXES: the Government had already bought the Khedive's Suez Canal shares; the House had not yet voted the money; and its own envoy's examination of Egyptian finances was still running. The Marquess of Hartington asked the Chancellor of the Exchequer, in the Prime Minister's absence, "Whether he will lay upon the Table of the House the Instructions to Mr. Cave in regard to his mission to Egypt, and any Correspondence between Her Majesty's Government and the Government of the Khedive on the subject of that mission?", and whether the Government would "ask the House on Monday evening to proceed to take the Vote" or "give the House another opportunity of considering the statement". THE CHANCELLOR'S ANSWER CONTAINS THE KEY ADMISSION: "As to the first Question, Sir, of the noble Lord, the mission of Mr. Cave is not yet completed; but there will be no objection to lay upon the Table of the House the Correspondence between the Government and the Khedive which led to the appointment of that mission and the instructions to Mr. Cave. Those Papers shall be printed in the course of this evening, and will, I hope, be in the hands of hon. Members before the discussion comes on on this subject on Monday night." So the instructions and the covering correspondence were to be laid; the report of what the envoy found was not, because the mission was still unfinished. On the concessions themselves the Chancellor added that the papers "relating to the Concessions of the Company and to the Firmans by which those Concessions were granted, will be prepared and laid before the House, although I am afraid that it will take some time before that can be done", directing Members meanwhile to "Volumes 55 and 56 of Hertslet's State Papers, which are in the Library." WHAT IS NOT HERE: no price, no valuation of the shares, nothing about the Khedive's solvency, and no figure of any kind. Hansard identifies the speakers only by office and title, and this dossier does not name the individuals holding those offices, because this page does not.

citations.title: House of Commons, "THE SUEZ CANAL SHARES—COMMISSIONS.—QUESTION.", HC Deb 29 February 1876 vol 227 c1120 (Historic Hansard)
citations.quoteOrFact: Read in full on Parliament's own Historic Hansard service; the whole exchange is two sentences long and is quoted here complete. MR. WILSON "asked Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer Whether he can inform the House whether the Khedive of Egypt paid a commission to agents in Egypt on the sale of the Canal shares to the English Government; and, if so, the amount of the commission?" THE CHANCELLOR OF THE EXCHEQUER "in reply, said, he had no information on that subject; but he would be exceedingly surprised if anything of the kind stated in the Question had occurred." THAT IS THE ENTIRE ANSWER. The question of who was paid to arrange the transaction was put to the minister who arranged it, eight days after the money was voted, and answered with an absence of information and an expression of surprise. NOTHING FURTHER IS ESTABLISHED: this page does not show that any commission was paid, or that none was. It shows that the question was asked and that the Government did not answer it. Any claim that a commission was in fact paid, or to whom, is outside what was read and is not asserted by this dossier.

citations.title: House of Commons, "EGYPTIAN FINANCE—MR. CAVE'S REPORT.—QUESTION.", HC Deb 23 March 1876 vol 228 c480 (Historic Hansard)
citations.quoteOrFact: Read in full on Parliament's own Historic Hansard service. This is the refusal, and the stated reason for it is the thing worth preserving. MR. W. CARTWRIGHT "asked the First Lord of the Treasury, If he could say when the Report of Mr. Cave, on his mission, is likely to be presented?" MR. DISRAELI answered: "When I was last asked the Question on this subject, I said I had not seen the Report of Mr. Cave. Since then it has been sent to the Government, and I have had the advantage of reading it; but on reading it I felt—and that feeling was unanimously shared by my Colleagues—that it was necessary, first of all, to communicate with the Khedive on the question of the publication. That communication has been made, and the Khedive has expressed a strong objection to this Report being made public in the present unsettled condition of Egyptian finance; and, considering that much of the information contained in the Report has been supplied by the Khedive himself, and is of a confidential character, we feel bound to respect his wishes in this matter." THE STRUCTURE OF THAT ANSWER: the British Government's own report on the solvency of a sovereign debtor whose asset it had just bought was withheld from Parliament at the debtor's request, on the ground that publication would be inconvenient given "the present unsettled condition of Egyptian finance" — that is, withheld for the reason that made it worth reading. The decision is attributed to the Cabinet unanimously. TEN DAYS EARLIER, on 13 March 1876 (HC Deb vol 227 c1870), the same Prime Minister had told MR. J. W. BARCLAY that "he had not yet seen the Report, which, he understood, had only been delivered to the Foreign Office that afternoon. Perhaps the hon. Member would on a future day repeat the Question." That page was also read, on the Historic Hansard service, at /historic-hansard/commons/1876/mar/13/egyptian-finance-mr-caves-report-question.

citations.title: House of Commons, "EGYPTIAN FINANCE—MR. CAVE'S REPORT.—QUESTIONS.", HC Deb 28 March 1876 vol 228 cc699-700 (Historic Hansard)
citations.quoteOrFact: Read in full on Parliament's own Historic Hansard service. Five days after the refusal, two Members took the stated reason apart and the Government gave a different one. SIR GEORGE CAMPBELL "asked the First Lord of the Treasury, Whether Mr. Cave's Report is in the possession of the Khedive of Egypt; and, if so, whether Her Majesty's Government will consent to His Highness publishing the parts of the Report which he thinks proper to publish while other parts are kept back?" MR. DISRAELI: "The text of Mr. Cave's Report, I believe, is not yet in the possession of the Khedive of Egypt. The remainder of the inquiry of the hon. Gentleman is of a hypothetical character, and it is inconvenient, I think, generally to put such questions ... I have to state that no request of that kind has been made by His Highness to the Government." So the debtor whose strong objection had been given as the reason for suppression five days earlier did not, on the Prime Minister's own account, yet have the text. SIR H. DRUMMOND WOLFF then asked the Chancellor of the Exchequer, on private notice, "Whether he is in a position to state if the information on which Mr. Cave's Report is founded was supplied to him by the Khedive confidentially or with the understanding that the Report was to be published?" THE CHANCELLOR'S ANSWER CONTRADICTS THE GROUND GIVEN ON 23 MARCH: "The Question assumes that the Report was founded solely upon information given by the Khedive. Now, the Report was not founded solely upon information given by the Khedive, but upon that information and other information obtained by my right hon. Friend. It was no part of the duty of my right hon. Friend, in the mission with which he was charged, to prepare a Report for the purpose of being published. He was instructed to obtain certain information for the guidance and information of Her Majesty's Government. In the conversations which he had with the Khedive a good deal of information was given to him by his Highness—some of which, no doubt, was intended to be of a confidential character, while other such information was of a less confidential character." On 23 March the Report was withheld because its information came from the Khedive and was confidential; on 28 March it was not founded solely on his information, and the real reason offered is that it had never been meant for publication at all. Both statements are in the record, five days apart, and this dossier sets them side by side without resolving which was the operative reason.

citations.title: House of Commons, "THE EGYPTIAN DEBT—MR. CAVE'S REPORT.—QUESTION.", HC Deb 12 May 1876 vol 229 cc490-1 (Historic Hansard)
citations.quoteOrFact: Read in full on Parliament's own Historic Hansard service. By 12 May the Report was available to Members — Cave refers them to it — and the envoy answered for his own figures in person. MR. WILLIAM CARTWRIGHT "asked the right honourable Member for Shoreham, Whether his attention has been drawn to a discrepancy of £16,000,000, between the Estimate as to the Khedive's indebtedness in his own Report and that given in the Khedive's Decree of May 2, for a proposed unification of his liabilities; and, whether he has any reason to apprehend that he was misled when he put at £75,000,000 the whole indebtedness of the Khedive?" MR. STEPHEN CAVE replied: "Yes, Sir, my attention has been called to this apparent discrepancy, but the hon. Member does not state the case quite accurately. If he will refer to my Report he will see that the amount of £75,000,000 does not include three loans nearly paid off, amounting altogether to £5,000,000. The difference is thus reduced to £11,000,000. He will also see that I estimated the cost of conversion of the Debt, according to my own plan, at £2,000,000; but I calculate that the cost of conversion under the new scheme will be £7,000,000, by far the larger portion of which is given in the form of a bonus to the holders of Treasury bonds—for the purpose, I suppose, of floating the Debt. This difference will account for another £5,000,000, leaving £6,000,000 to be accounted for. Now, if we take £3,000,000 or £4,000,000 as the excess over the Estimate for the Abyssinian War—which is, of course, merely conjectural—we shall still have between £2,000,000 and £3,000,000 unaccounted for; and I cannot tell without further information whether this is due to any error in the information given to me or whether it is due to increased expenditure since that information was given." TWO THINGS HERE ARE WORTH MORE THAN THE ARITHMETIC. First, the Government's own envoy tells the House that between £2,000,000 and £3,000,000 of a sovereign's debt is "unaccounted for" and that he cannot say whether he was misinformed or whether the spending came later. Second, he identifies where £5,000,000 of the gap went, in his own words: the new conversion scheme cost £7,000,000 against his own plan's £2,000,000, "by far the larger portion of which is given in the form of a bonus to the holders of Treasury bonds—for the purpose, I suppose, of floating the Debt." That is the transfer, stated by the official who examined the books. WHAT IS NOT ESTABLISHED: the Report itself was not read for this dossier — only Cave's account of it in the House — and no bondholder, bank or agent is named anywhere in this exchange.
